rationale: Clinical abnormality in TUAB often shows up as an overall change in amplitude, such as diffuse slowing with high-amplitude delta/theta or suppression. Relative power hides this because it divides by total power. So I'm adding per-channel log absolute band power and log total power (all TUAB recordings use the same amplifier setup and are already average-referenced), computed with median-averaged Welch so short artifact bursts don't inflate it.

Clinical EEG abnormality in TUAB mostly shows up as slowing: the posterior dominant rhythm moves down in frequency and there is excess focal or diffuse delta and theta. Five broad bands blur these shifts, so I'm replacing them with a log-relative PSD in 1 Hz bins (1–45 Hz) per channel. The PSD uses median-averaged Welch, so the artifact-heavy clinical segments have less influence. Normalizing by total power keeps the features independent of amplitude scale. Because the feature count grows to 836, the L2 strength is now chosen by grouped inner CV on AUROC.

Relative band power divides out each channel's total power, so it throws away absolute amplitude. In TUAB, abnormal recordings often show high-amplitude slow activity and focal power changes, so I'm adding per-channel log absolute band power and log total 1–45 Hz power next to the existing relative features. The classifier stays the same, so any change in score comes from the new features. This hasn't been run here yet, so I don't have a Dev score for it.

I'm replacing the 5 broad bands with a finer log-relative spectrum (2-Hz bins from 1 to 45 Hz per channel). The aim is to capture abnormal-EEG markers that broad bands blur together: diffuse or focal slowing, a slower posterior alpha peak, and beta changes caused by medication. Because this gives about 4× more features, the L2 strength is now chosen with a grouped inner CV on the training fold, not fixed at C=0.1. I haven't run this here; the harness will score it.

I'm adding log absolute band power per channel alongside the existing relative power. Abnormal clinical EEGs often show diffuse or focal slowing and generally larger delta/theta amplitude. Relative power hides that total-amplitude information once each channel is normalized by its own total, and the TUAB data all come from one clinic and amplifier family, so absolute amplitude should be a reliable cue.

Five coarse relative bands throw away most of the spectral detail. Abnormal clinical EEG shows up as specific shifts: focal or diffuse slowing, a slower or weaker posterior alpha peak, and changes in overall amplitude. So I'm replacing the per-channel mean Welch spectrum with a median-averaged one, which resists the many artifacts in these unprocessed recordings. I add log absolute power in 1-Hz bins from 1 to 45 Hz alongside the existing relative band powers, and pick the logistic-regression C by grouped inner CV on the training fold, because the feature set is now much larger.

Relative power throws away overall amplitude, but abnormal clinical EEGs often show high-amplitude slowing and suppressed or diffusely raised power. So I'm adding per-channel log absolute band power, and computing all features with median-averaged Welch so that short high-amplitude artifact segments don't dominate the spectrum.

I'm replacing the 5 coarse relative bands with a log power spectrum at 1-Hz resolution (1–45 Hz) for every channel. Each spectrum is computed with median-averaged Welch, which resists artifacts. This keeps the absolute power level, which captures diffuse slowing and changes in amplitude. It also keeps the fine spectral shape, such as alpha-peak shifts, beta excess and the 1/f slope, which coarse relative bands throw away. With 19 × 45 features, the logistic regression's L2 strength C is chosen by grouped inner CV on the training fold.

I'm swapping the five coarse bands for a 1-Hz-resolution log spectrum per channel (1–45 Hz, divided by total power), plus each channel's log total power. Abnormal clinical EEG shows narrow slowing, a slower alpha peak and broad changes in overall power, and fixed band edges blur these. Because this gives about 870 features from about 2,700 recordings, I pick the logistic regression penalty with an inner patient-grouped CV on the training fold instead of fixing it.

Five broad relative bands throw away most of the spectral detail. Abnormal clinical EEG shows up as focal or diffuse slowing, a slower or shifted posterior dominant rhythm and excess beta. These are narrow-band effects that also depend on overall power, so I replace the 5 bands with a 1-Hz-resolution log relative spectrum (1–45 Hz) plus log total power per channel. The Welch average is a median, which resists artifacts, and the logistic-regression C is tuned by grouped inner CV for the larger feature set.

Two of the main signs of an abnormal clinical EEG are diffuse or focal slowing and a slower posterior alpha rhythm. Both are frequency shifts that the 5 coarse bands mostly average away. This change replaces the bands with relative log-power in 1-Hz bins (1–45 Hz) for each channel. Because that gives about 840 features, the L2 logistic regression's C is now picked by grouped inner CV on the training fold.

Five coarse relative bands throw away two things: the absolute amplitude and the shape of the spectrum within each band. Both matter for clinical abnormality (focal or diffuse slowing, low or high amplitude, loss of the alpha peak, a shifted beta). This round replaces them with a robust median-Welch log absolute spectrum in 1 Hz bins from 1 to 45 Hz per channel, plus total power. The median makes it resistant to the unrejected artifacts. The L2-logistic regularization strength is picked by grouped inner CV on the training fold because the feature count grows from 95 to about 855.

Five coarse relative bands per channel throw away most of the spectrum. Abnormal clinical EEG shows up as focal or diffuse slowing, extra amplitude, and changes in the alpha and beta shape that don't line up with fixed band edges. So I'm replacing the band powers with the full 1-Hz-resolution log PSD (1–45 Hz) per channel, both absolute and relative. Each PSD is the median across Welch segments, so artifacts don't skew it. The model stays an L2 logistic regression, with its strength C picked by grouped inner CV on the training fold, which matters now that there are many more features.

I'm replacing the 5 coarse bands with relative log-power in fine 1-Hz bins from 1 to 45 Hz per channel. The PSD uses a median-averaged Welch estimate, so short artifact bursts in these unrejected clinical recordings carry less weight. The features stay amplitude-scale invariant for the external sets, and the L2 strength is tuned by grouped inner CV on the training fold, since the features grow from 95 to 836. I'm adding log absolute band power per channel (the same five bands plus log total 1–45 Hz power) alongside the existing relative features. In clinical EEG, abnormal recordings often show diffuse or focal slowing as a rise in absolute delta/theta power and a change in overall amplitude. Relative power divides that information out, so it can't use it. TUAB recordings share an amplifier pipeline and are all average-referenced, so absolute power should be comparable across recordings. The standardized L2 logistic regression model stays as it is, so the only thing that changes is this feature family.

I'm replacing the 5 coarse relative bands with the full log-absolute spectrum in 1-Hz bins (1–45 Hz, every channel), and choosing the regularization strength with grouped inner CV. Abnormal clinical EEG mostly shows up as slowing: a lower alpha peak frequency and extra delta/theta, often focal and with changed amplitude. Fixed band edges blur a shifted alpha peak, and relative power discards the absolute amplitude information.

I'm replacing the five fixed bands with a finer relative spectrum: 22 log relative-power bins, each 2 Hz wide from 1 to 45 Hz, per channel. The spectra are estimated with median-averaged Welch, which resists clipped or movement-artifact segments in unclean clinical recordings. Abnormal EEG shows up as slowing, loss of the alpha rhythm, peak-frequency shifts and beta changes, and fixed band edges blur all of these, especially between subjects. The regularization strength C is now chosen by grouped inner CV on the training fold, because the feature dimension grew from 95 to 418.

Five wide bands may blur the spectral signs that matter in clinical abnormality (focal or diffuse slowing, a slower or weaker posterior rhythm, fast beta from medication), and relative power also discards amplitude. This version uses per-channel log absolute PSD in 1-Hz bins (1–45 Hz) plus the log total power. The PSD uses median-averaged Welch so artifact segments have less pull. The L2 strength is picked by grouped inner CV on the training fold.

Abnormal clinical EEG mostly shows up as focal or diffuse slowing and changes in overall amplitude. Relative band power over 5 broad bands removes absolute amplitude and blurs the spectral shape. This round adds per-channel log absolute PSD in 1-Hz bins (1–45 Hz) alongside the existing relative band powers. Because the feature count grows, the logistic regression's C is now tuned by inner grouped CV on the training fold.

Five coarse bands blur the signs that mark an abnormal clinical EEG, such as focal or diffuse slowing, a slowed or missing posterior alpha peak, and fast beta from medication. I'm replacing them with a scale-free relative log-spectrum in 2 Hz bins from 1 to 45 Hz per channel. The PSD uses median-averaged Welch so it is less sensitive to artifacts, and the L2 strength is chosen by patient-grouped inner CV to fit the larger number of features.
